source_text: So, my one caution is that we shouldn't "improve" the behaviour of Lean4, given that we're  trying to emulate it.  If we find problems with the way Lean4 does things, then we should submit patches over there.  I'm not sure if this consideration applies, I'm just saying, what we've done does sound like we haven't (yet) strictly emulated Lean and are (instead) on the path to doing so, which is good!  >>> blank startup unconditionally compiles 14 structurally selected declarations, including `mkOptConfig`/`appendConfig`; native Lean instead installs module-initializer effects and runs only the empty-stream parser path

reply_text:
㊥ (emulate, don't improve) Agreed, and I've saved it as a standing rule: if Lean does something wrong, the fix goes upstream to Lean as a patch, not into the port. The broader ROOTS rule doesn't count as an improvement. It moves the port's startup closer to what Lean does: install the initializer effects, then run only the parser path the input needs. Compiling a body when it is first needed is the port's version of Lean loading precompiled code, so the results stay the same as Lean's.

㊟ (where the rule needs watching) Changes that alter what a user sees are where an "improvement" could slip in. The one live case is codex-6's APPINST job: when an instance problem is stuck on unsolved metavariables, it errors instead of silently picking an arbitrary instance. From memory, Lean also errors here ("typeclass instance problem is stuck, it is often due to metavariables"), so this should be matching Lean, not improving on it. I haven't checked the source line this turn. When the job reports back, I'll require it to cite the Lean code before I accept it.

㊢ (what I recorded) The rule is now in my memory file `lean-is-the-source-of-truth-for-port-fixes.md` and its index line. Future job briefs will repeat it.

Checking whether the 3 failures in codex-6's branch were already there before its change. I'm running the same tests on the base commit.Holding pattern isn't needed: the gate tests show no regression, so I'm applying the guard to startup-linux.Same three failures as on the base commit. Pushing the fork, and recording the result.㊥ (codex-6's instance job) codex-6 stopped once it had found the cause, as the brief told it to. When the port resolves type-class instances inside an expression, it does so before it knows the types of the operands, which is the reverse of Lean's order. Fixing that needs one shared argument elaborator, and that is a bigger job than the brief allowed. What it kept is a small guard: when the instance problem still contains unknowns, the port now reports `typeclass instance problem is stuck` instead of silently picking `String.Pos.Raw`. I've put that on startup-linux as `816eb3b` and pushed the fork.

㊢ (where the cause sits, from APPINST.md) The failing expression is `size % 2 == 0` at `Init/Data/List/Notation.lean:58-61`, inside the `term[_]` macro. The port reaches application compilation by two separate routes, and `%` and `==` come in through the notation-expansion one. Lean elaborates the explicit arguments first and synthesizes the instances afterwards (`Lean/Elab/App.lean`). In the port, `size`'s type `Nat` never reaches the unifier. The fix would make both routes call one argument elaborator, which touches at least five places. This only matters once `term[_]` is actually needed. codex-4's classification job is meant to take it out of blank startup.

㊬ (what I checked) I read the net diff: it is 29 lines across two files, the guard plus one regression test. I ran `instance_synthesis_test.py` on the base commit `8208d96`, on codex-6's branch and on startup-linux. The same three tests fail in all three, so those failures were already there. On the branch, the coercion-resolution file passes. I did not rerun the cold startup. codex-6's diagnostic run took 270 s, peaked at 2.7 GiB, had no OOM, and stopped at the new error. Its trial commits are kept as `fork/appinst-discovery`.

㊩ (against your emulate-don't-improve point) The guard is stricter than Lean in one respect. It rejects every unknown, but Lean still solves problems whose unknowns are only in `outParam` positions, and it tries default instances before it reports "stuck". No run has hit that case yet, and the port has no table of which class arguments are outParams on this path. I've noted the gap in the commit message and in PLAN.md. If a run does hit it, the result is a loud error rather than a wrong instance.

㊢ (still running) codex-4: classification fix plus a cold run (`park-e10826d1`). zai-3: K1 token kinds (`park-2a00569d`).

Parking on the write-up request now.㊥ (zai-3 token kinds, deadline) I've stopped zai-3's token-kind measurement and asked it to write up what it has. It had got through 200 of 1,084 declarations in 35 minutes, and 152 of those 200 had errored. Its own 80-minute timeout would have ended it at about 460, so it could not have finished. Write-up request: `invoke-…c1137817`, parked as `park-8bc23673` with a 50-minute backstop.

㊢ (what the log showed) The 152 errors break down as:
- 80 ImportError
- 49 ValueError. 28 of these are "conflicting Lean source owners": the run picked up Lean source paths from two worktrees, `/tmp/mfs-real` and `/tmp/mfs-map2`, through the symlinked `tools/lean4`.
- 24 module-shape errors
- 7 link errors
- 5 imported-dependency demands

Earlier, at 10:46, zai-3 had noted that all 876 grammar kinds fail with the compiler's fail-closed error.

🈖 (why I stopped it) The measurement is a side map, and its errors were not getting fewer. The brief told zai-3 to list failures and not patch the source, so letting it run longer would only produce more of the same errors. I've asked for four things:
- which production function it called;
- whatever token kinds it collected;
- the errors grouped by cause;
- its judgement on whether these kinds can be measured without a real startup at all.

My expectation is that K1 moves back to "measure from a real startup", like K3a.

㊟ (process) Killing the process was my call, since I dispatched the work. The process was running without the 12G memory scope: 6.6 GiB resident, and an earlier run reached 8.8 GB. There was plenty of free memory, so no harm came of it, but the next long run will go through bg.py.

㊢ (still running) codex-4: classification fix plus a cold run (`park-e10826d1`).

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (your JIT remark) Yes. Under the ROOTS.md rule, a blank file would compile almost nothing in advance: a declaration body would be compiled only when the parser reaches it. Lean doesn't need that, because it loads precompiled code and only runs the initializers. The port compiles from source, so compiling on first use is how it would match Lean. Shall I give that broader rule to a seat once codex-4's narrower run reports?

previous_reply_acts.text: (limits of the claim) ROOTS.md expects `term[_]` to drop out of blank startup under either step. That is a prediction, not a measurement. codex-4's cold run will test it for the narrow step. The broader rule is not implemented, and I haven't put it to Rob yet.
